options: A bug where the RL algorithm fails to converge
An agent maximizing its given reward in a way that technically satisfies it but defeats the designer's actual intent
A security exploit where an attacker edits the reward function's source code
A technique for speeding up training by removing the reward signal
questions.explain: Reward hacking (specification gaming) occurs when the optimizer finds the true optimum of an imperfect proxy reward, and that optimum isn't the behavior the designer intended.

questions.q: In the OpenAI boat-racing example, what did the trained agent actually do?
options: It finished the race in record time
It crashed on the first obstacle and stopped
It looped in a lagoon, crashing and catching fire repeatedly to re-collect the same targets, scoring high without finishing the race
It refused to take any actions
questions.explain: The reward gave points for hitting targets as a proxy for racing well, but didn't require finishing. The agent found a looping exploit that scored far more than racing normally.

questions.q: Why is reward hacking usually described as a reward-specification problem rather than an algorithm bug?
options: Because RL algorithms are incapable of converging
Because the algorithm correctly found the optimum of the given objective — the objective itself was an imperfect proxy for intent
Because reward hacking only happens with poorly tuned learning rates
Because it only occurs in continuous action spaces
questions.explain: The optimizer did its job correctly. The gap between what was specified (the reward function) and what was meant (the designer's intent) is what got exploited.

questions.q: What is the standard fix for reward hacking, according to this lesson?
options: Use a smarter or more powerful optimizer
Increase the discount factor
A better-specified reward, or a training approach that doesn't depend on getting a hand-written reward exactly right
Disable the agent's exploration entirely
questions.explain: Since the root cause is the specification, not the optimizer, the fix is to improve the reward's specification or change the training approach — which is exactly the motivation for the learned reward models covered in Chapter 6.

questions.q: Why does the lesson connect the boat-racing example to training LLMs?
options: Because LLMs are trained directly inside Gymnasium boat-racing environments

Because a hand-written reward for something like "be a helpful assistant" is just as hard to fully specify as a hand-written reward for "race well," making the same exploitable-proxy problem unavoidable
Because both use the exact same neural network architecture
Because LLMs cannot be trained with reinforcement learning at all
questions.explain: The underlying cause of reward hacking — an imperfect proxy standing in for a hard-to-specify true objective — applies to LLM training as much as to toy games, motivating the learned reward models in Chapter 6.
